paras: The attempted lynchings of Joe Scott were two attempts by armed crowds in Chippewa County, Minnesota, in July 1903 to take Scott, a Black man accused of an axe assault on a white woman, from officers; Black residents were also driven from Montevideo. Officers held off several hundred men at the Montevideo depot on July 19 and outran a second mob from Minnesota Falls on July 22. Scott pleaded guilty in November and was sentenced to thirty years.

Early on July 18, 1903, an intruder entered Thomas Olson's house at Watson, Chippewa County, where his daughter Helen was staying with Julia Torgenson. According to the first reports, he demanded money and struck Olson on the forehead with an axe; doctors said she would die.

At Montevideo the town bells were rung and Sheriff Hartley deputized the assembled men to hunt for a man "supposed to be a negro." The Associated Press predicted a lynching and reported that six Black men living near Montevideo had fled.

A posse caught Scott on the afternoon of July 18 near Milan, shooting him in the arm as he ran. Chief of Police Denny of Ortonville and deputies guarded him with rifles in an empty coach of an excursion train. When the train reached Montevideo, the Bemidji Daily Pioneer reported, several hundred men armed with rifles, revolvers and shotguns, some carrying ropes, were on the platform "clamoring for the negro's life." The crowd rushed the car, but Denny threatened to shoot the first man who boarded, and the train went on to the Glencoe jail.
That night several Black residents were driven out of Montevideo by what the St. Paul Globe called "an infuriated mob"; the Willmar Tribune said they were given twenty-four hours to leave.

On July 22 Sheriffs Hartley and McKenzie took Scott by train from Glencoe toward a preliminary hearing in Chippewa County. At Minnesota Falls a crowd met the train and demanded the prisoner, and the sheriffs, revolvers drawn, forced their way to a buggy. The Morris Tribune described "a thousand angry and excited men and boys" and a hand-to-hand fight before the sheriffs escaped. After a farmhouse hearing at which Scott was bound over, the sheriffs outran the mob, which gave up near Bird Island.

Olson survived and slowly improved after an operation on her skull. Scott, recently out of prison, had a Black Minneapolis attorney expected to plead insanity, and Governor Van Sant offered troops for the trial.

On November 24 Scott pleaded guilty at Montevideo and was sentenced to thirty years in the penitentiary. According to the Globe, a crowd that "filled the court house and crowded the streets" followed him to the train.

The Associated Press carried the story nationally from the first day, and headlines in white papers called Scott a "NEGRO FIEND" and a "NEGRO BRUTE." The Wheeling Sunday Register's headline said he "OUTRAGED HER" and the Evening Star called him a "Negro Rapist," though the reports described a robbery and an axe blow. Minnesota editors split: the Minneapolis Journal called the depot crowd "an outbreak of the spirit of disorder," while the Mankato Free Press asked whether it was "any wonder" people took "the law into their own hands."

In the Black press, the Cleveland Gazette ran the Glencoe wire on July 25, and the State Ledger printed it a month later as "Prospect is Good for a Lynching in Minnesota." Reporting the sentence, the St. Paul Appeal wrote that there had been "no attempt to commit rape, although the papers at the time endeavored to create the impression that there was," though it called the sentence "deserved." In September the Deseret Evening News printed Mormon elders' letter saying the mob, denied its prisoner, threatened the missionaries.

A Montevideo dispatch to the Globe denied there had been a mob: the depot crowd was "merely a lot of curious boys and possibly a few crippled old men," and schoolmates had only asked the Black residents to leave. Officers and other dispatches describe an armed crowd held back by guns and an expulsion by a mob.
Reports also differ on the victim's first name and on the size of the Minnesota Falls crowd.

reader.title: Attempted lynchings of Joe Scott and expulsion of Black residents from Montevideo, Minnesota
bases: Armed crowds twice tried to take Joe Scott, a Black man accused of an axe assault, from sheriffs to lynch him, at the Montevideo depot (A6, A9, A10) and at Minnesota Falls (A11, A17, A19); the same days saw Black residents driven out of Montevideo (A6, A10, A12).

Crowds of several hundred (A6, A9) and, by one report, a thousand (A19) sought to lynch Scott over the assault on Helen Olson, but officers kept him from them and he was later sentenced in court (A28); no one was killed, so this is an attempted lynching, not a lynching.

Separate Montevideo, Glencoe and Watson dispatches in several papers agree that armed crowds tried to reach Scott at Montevideo and Minnesota Falls (A6, A9, A11, A17, A19), and the Black press carried the second attempt (A18, A24); a Montevideo rebuttal disputes the size and nature of the depot crowd (A12).

accounts.label: Wire and Minnesota dispatches
accounts.gist: Hundreds of armed men with ropes met the train at Montevideo and rushed the car, and a second mob at Minnesota Falls fought the sheriffs and chased them; only the officers' guns and the mob's lack of a leader saved Scott.

accounts.label: Montevideo correspondent
accounts.gist: There was no organized mob: the armed men were a lawful sheriff's posse, the depot crowd was curious boys and old men, and schoolboys merely asked the few Black residents to leave.

accounts.label: Black press
accounts.gist: The Cleveland Gazette and State Ledger ran the wire on the mob chasing the sheriffs; the St. Paul Appeal reported the sentence and said there had been no attempted rape.

accounts.label: Mormon missionaries
accounts.gist: A mob gathered to lynch a Black man who had 'murdered' a young lady and, when he was kept away, threatened the Mormon elders.

framing.detail: News headlines branded Scott a 'NEGRO FIEND' and 'NEGRO BRUTE' and some implied rape ('WHO OUTRAGED HER', 'Negro Rapist'), while praising the officers who held off the mob.
The Minneapolis Journal's 'The Lynching Habit' called the depot mob an outbreak of 'the spirit of disorder' in the state.
The Mankato Free Press attacked the insanity defense and asked whether it was 'any wonder' that people 'take the law into their own hands'.
A Montevideo dispatch to the Globe denied a mob existed and recast the expulsion as schoolboys' request.
The Cleveland Gazette and State Ledger reprinted the Glencoe wire without comment, the Ledger under 'Prospect is Good for a Lynching in Minnesota'.
The St. Paul Appeal rejected the rape insinuation but called the sentence 'deserved' and Scott a discredit to the race.

info: The assault on Helen Olson took place early Saturday, July 18, 1903 (the Globe's later account says the night of July 17); the depot confrontation at Montevideo was early Sunday, July 19; the second attempt at Minnesota Falls was Wednesday, July 22; a crowd gathered again at the plea and sentencing at Montevideo on Tuesday, November 24.
Assault at Watson, Chippewa county; capture near Milan; mob at the Montevideo railroad depot; second mob at Minnesota Falls, pursuit as far as Bird Island; Scott held at Glencoe, McLeod county.
Joe (Joseph) Scott, a Black man, the target of the lynching attempts; also the Black residents of Montevideo who were driven out or told to leave.

Accused of breaking into the Olson house at Watson to rob it and striking Helen Olson on the head with an axe; bound over on first-degree assault and burglary; he confessed to robbery and the axe blow. Some white headlines called it an outrage or rape; the St. Paul Appeal said there was no attempt at rape.

Crowds of white townspeople of the Montevideo area (not named), described as armed with rifles, revolvers, shotguns and ropes; at Minnesota Falls 'men and boys'. The expulsion of Black residents was attributed to a mob or, in a Montevideo rebuttal, to Olson's schoolmates.
Scott pleaded guilty at Montevideo and was sentenced to thirty years in the penitentiary at Stillwater.
